solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Suddenly attack American submarine around the opening of Hormuz

indicators.note: around means turned round, so the boat word is read backwards

parts.note: a sub is the everyday short name for a submarine, as a U-boat is

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Hormuz is H

explanation.surface: An American submarine launches a surprise strike near the Strait of Hormuz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' looks like a containment signal, but nothing goes inside; it turns the boat backwards, to BUS, and 'the opening of' Hormuz adds its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambush is a surprise attack launched from a concealed position, and the word is also the verb.

clue.text: Three articles eviscerating Madonna? That's an abomination!

parts.note: the articles AN, A and THE

indicators.note: gutting Madonna removes her insides, leaving only the outer letters

parts.note: MADONNA with its insides removed leaves M…A

explanation.surface: An outraged critic reviewing magazine pieces that tear the pop star Madonna apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' reads as newspaper pieces savaging the singer; in grammar the articles are A, AN and THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Originally a church curse, the word now names anything loathed, so 'an abomination' is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Rotten time to engage in playful talk

indicators.note: to engage is to hold or take in, as one gear engages another, so the outer word takes the smaller one inside

parts.note: rotten = bad
an age = a period of time
the word itself, taken in

explanation.surface: Someone grumbling that it is a bad moment to start bantering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engage in' reads as one phrasal verb; split it, and 'in' becomes the very letters that get engaged.
explanation.definitionFit: Badinage is light, teasing, playful conversation.

clue.text: Diminished newspaper relying on Kelvin?

parts.note: The Sun, a British tabloid
K = kelvin, the unit of temperature

explanation.surface: A shrunken newspaper leaning on someone called Kelvin to keep it afloat.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue SUN sits on top of K, so 'relying on' describes the stacking. The Sun is a British daily tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sunk has gone down, fallen to a lower level, diminished.

clue.text: Expert/ace crew member catching flatfish

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it, so the outer letters close around the fish

parts.note: A = ace, as on playing cards
a hand is a member of a ship's crew
a dab is a small flatfish

explanation.surface: A skilled deckhand on a fishing boat hauling in a flatfish.
explanation.walkthrough: The slash shows 'Expert' and 'ace' are two separate words, not one phrase; only 'Expert' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A British informal idiom for someone very skilled at something, as in being handy in the kitchen.

clue.text: Store license's date ran out

indicators.note: the letters run off in disorder

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper worried because their trading licence has expired.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is ignored, so the S counts as a letter of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A delicatessen is a shop selling prepared foods.

clue.text: Blair urges reforms to petty crimes

indicators.note: the letters are re-formed into something new

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: Tony Blair, the former British prime minister, calling for changes to the law on minor offences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reforms' fits a politician so well it reads as policy; here it turns the letters over.
explanation.definitionFit: Burglaries are break-in thefts, crimes against property.

clue.text: Acknowledge Laycock regularly noted record temperature

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals: lAyCoCk

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters of LAYCOCK
EP = extended-play record
T = temperature

explanation.surface: Admitting that a man called Laycock routinely logged a record high temperature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record temperature' wants to be a heatwave headline; it splits into EP and T.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean admitting that something is so, as when you concede a point.

clue.text: Sweet song Leonard Cohen initially penned

indicators.note: penned means shut in, so the initials are enclosed by the song

parts.note: a duet is a song for two voices

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each name gives its first letter

parts.note: the first letters of Leonard and Cohen are L and C

explanation.surface: A sweet song that the singer Leonard Cohen wrote early in his career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penned' looks like 'wrote', fitting a songwriter, but it means enclosed: the initials L and C are penned in the song.
explanation.definitionFit: Dulcet describes a sound that is sweet and soothing to the ear, as in dulcet tones.

clue.text: Burning area of forest close to Stockport

parts.note: the Forest of Arden, in Warwickshire, England

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter

parts.note: last letter of Stockport

explanation.surface: A report of a woodland fire near Stockport, a town in Greater Manchester.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' reads as 'near' Stockport; it means the town's final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ardent literally means burning, and figuratively passionate.

clue.text: Start to clean large, lacier pants belonging to the vicar?

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of clean is C
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the letters are a mess, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sets about washing a large pair of the vicar's lacy knickers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' looks like underwear, matching 'lacier'; it is British slang for rubbish, so it rearranges LACIER into ERICAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Clerical means relating to the clergy, so a vicar's things are clerical ones.

clue.text: One used to hear a call for order?

definitions.meaning: really a telephone call you listen to through a loudspeaker, hands free
reads as the Speaker of the House of Commons shouting 'Order!' to calm MPs

explanation.surface: A riddle about the device, or person, you hear a demand for order through.
explanation.walkthrough: A speakerphone lets you hear a phone call; 'call for order' also suggests the Speaker of the House of Commons calling 'Order!'.
explanation.definitionFit: A speakerphone is a telephone you hear a call on without holding it.

clue.text: Sharpen new garden tool outside

indicators.note: one word placed outside another wraps round it, so the tool surrounds the single letter

parts.note: a hoe is a weeding tool
N = new

explanation.surface: A gardener sharpening a new tool out in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' sits naturally with gardening, suggesting outdoors; it places HOE around N.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the hone, a whetstone used to put an edge on blades.

clue.text: A Pepsi cola one's left for Yankee ordered in The World's End

indicators.note: ordered in means arranged into, so the letters are put into a new order
one has left and made way for the Yankee letter, which takes its place

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one; one's reads as one has
Y is Yankee in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An American swaps his soft drink while ordering at a pub called The World's End.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one's left for Yankee' swaps the I of A PEPSI COLA for Y, giving APEPSYCOLA, which 'ordered in' rearranges. The World's End sounds like a pub name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Apocalypse is the prophesied final destruction of the world, its end in Revelation.

clue.text: Baroque composer taking time out over new advanced infection

indicators.note: in a down clue the composer goes over, above, the letters that follow
taking the time letter out of the name removes it
out completes taking out, the instruction to remove the time letter

parts.note: Domenico Scarlatti was a Baroque composer of keyboard sonatas
A stands for advanced, as in A level

explanation.surface: A Baroque composer takes a break while a new, serious illness sets in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking time out' removes one T from SCARLATTI, leaving SCARLATI; 'over' stacks it above N and A in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarlatina is another name for scarlet fever, a bacterial infection with a red rash.

clue.text: Mum, Joe and family rent refurbished projector

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mum
a GI Joe is an American soldier, so Joe gives GI
a clan is a family group

indicators.note: refurbished means done up anew, so the letters are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: Mum, Joe and the rest of the family rent a done-up projector.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like a verb sharing the family's action; it is fodder, and 'refurbished' turns it into TERN.
explanation.definitionFit: A magic lantern is an early image projector that cast pictures from glass slides.

clue.text: Empty flipping hollow before you had dinner?

indicators.note: the flipped word comes before the rest
flipping means turning over, so the hollow word is read backwards

parts.note: a cave is a hollow in rock
U is text-speak for you
ate means had a meal, had dinner

explanation.surface: Someone empties out a hollowed-out space before sitting down to dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' sounds like an exasperated British intensifier, as in 'flipping hollow'; it is the signal to read CAVE backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To evacuate a building or a container is to empty it, clearing everyone or everything out.

clue.text: Sign of star broadcaster is khaki trousers

indicators.note: as a verb, to trouser is to pocket, so the phrase holds the answer

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the first word across 'is' into the start of the third

explanation.surface: A star presenter recognised by their khaki trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' reads as clothing; used as a verb it means pockets, and the phrase before it pockets the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The asterisk is the little star-shaped sign in print.

clue.text: Folk song's eco-friendly record covers

parts.note: green = environmentally friendly
record sleeves are the covers of vinyl albums

explanation.surface: A folk song released on vinyl in recycled sleeves.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Tudor ballad, legendarily by Henry VIII, is England's best-known folk tune.

clue.text: Privy near bottom of street

parts.note: close = near

indicators.note: in a down clue the bottom of a word is its last letter

parts.note: last letter of street

explanation.surface: Directions to a toilet at the far end of the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Privy' looks like the noun for an outdoor toilet; as an adjective it means secret, like closet.
explanation.definitionFit: Privy and closet both mean secret or private, as in a closet admirer.

clue.text: Show Gene Vincent hosts

indicators.note: the phrase hosts the answer inside it

parts.note: the last letter of the first name runs on into the first five of the surname

explanation.surface: Gene Vincent, the 1950s rock and roll singer, presenting a TV show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' and 'hosts' look like television; show is the verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain, rather formal synonym: you reveal or display a quality, as in evincing surprise.

clue.text: Slav people produced veg

indicators.note: the letters are made into something new

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: A Slavic community growing its own vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: Love apple is an old name for the tomato.
explanation.definitionFit: Love apples are tomatoes, eaten as vegetables.

clue.text: Top Conservative featured in naked cameo

indicators.note: CAMEO stripped of its outer letters

parts.note: CAMEO without its first and last letters
C = Conservative, the British party

explanation.surface: A leading Tory politician appearing in a brief nude film role.
explanation.walkthrough: C goes after the A of AME, making A-C-ME.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the Greek for a point: the peak or height of something.

clue.text: Silly idea periodically supported by this paper

indicators.note: in a down clue the first part is held up by the paper's letters below it
periodically means at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of idea are D and A
FT is the Financial Times, the paper printing the puzzle

explanation.surface: A foolish notion now and then gets backing from this newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this paper' refers to the Financial Times, where the puzzle appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: Daft is a British informal word meaning silly, foolish or senseless.

clue.text: The club I go to when I'm splashing out?

definitions.meaning: reads as a nightclub or members' club; really a golf club
reads as spending lavishly; really blasting the ball out of a bunker in a spray of sand

explanation.surface: Someone naming the nightclub they head for when spending freely.
explanation.walkthrough: A golfer in a bunker splashes the ball out with sand; 'club' and 'splashing out' pretend to mean a nightspot and a spree.
explanation.definitionFit: A sand iron is a golf club, the sand wedge, for playing out of bunkers.

clue.text: Son returns service in first-class big game experience

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: S = son

indicators.note: 'in' puts one thing inside another, so the reversed service sits within first-class

parts.note: A1 = first-class, written with I for 1
the Royal Air Force, one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A son coming back to serve in a top-flight match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returns service' and 'big game' read as tennis; 'service' is the RAF, and 'big game' means wild animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A safari is an expedition to see or hunt big game.

clue.text: Youngster ate green bananas

indicators.note: slang for crazy, so the letters go wild

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A child eating unripe bananas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green bananas' reads as unripe fruit; 'green' is fodder and 'bananas' means crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: A teenager is a youngster aged thirteen to nineteen.

clue.text: Karts wheeling round Silverstone at the back barely run

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go round the final letter
wheeling means turning about, so the letters of karts are rearranged
at the back means the last letter of the word

parts.note: the last letter of Silverstone is E

explanation.surface: Go-karts racing around the back of the Silverstone circuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wheeling' rearranges KARTS as STR-AK around E. Silverstone is the British Grand Prix motor-racing circuit. 'barely' means naked here.
explanation.definitionFit: To streak is to run naked through a public place, so it is to run in the bare.
